opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it mostly comes down to a mismatch between what a launch document is for and what a research paper is for.

When you write a paper about a new evaluation, you're making a fairly strong claim: this eval measures the thing we say it measures. To back that up properly you want a lot of supporting work. You want to show the eval is valid, that a high score corresponds to the real-world capability or risk you care about. You want ablations, different elicitation methods, comparisons across models, error analysis, maybe human baselines. You want to describe the methodology in enough detail that someone else could critique or replicate it. That takes months, and it should, because that's how you build justified confidence in a new measurement.

A model card or frontier safety report at launch serves a different purpose. It's a snapshot: here's the model, here's what we tested, here's what we found, here's why we think it's okay to deploy. It's tied to a release timeline, and that timeline doesn't wait for a new eval to mature into a polished research artifact. If anything, the newest evals are the ones you're least sure about, because you built them recently, often specifically because the previous generation of evals was saturating or no longer captured the risks you're worried about.

So you're in an awkward spot. The evals most relevant to the frontier are the ones you've had the least time to validate. You can either leave them out, which seems worse because you lose information, or include them with a short description and a lot of implicit "trust us, we thought about this." Usually the right call is to include them, but you can't realistically give each one the treatment a standalone paper would get. There's also simply limited space. A safety report covering many risk areas can't devote twenty pages to every new benchmark.

There are some other constraints too. Some evals are deliberately kept partly private, either because publishing the details would contaminate future training data and make the eval useless, or because in areas like bio or cyber the specific content is itself somewhat hazardous. That limits how much methodological detail you can share regardless of time.

What I'd like to see, and what I think is the reasonable path, is treating the launch report as one stage in a longer process. At launch you report results with honest caveats about how mature each eval is. Then over time the more important evals get written up properly, with full methodology, validation, and external scrutiny where possible. External evaluators and third-party testing help as well, because they provide an independent check that doesn't depend on the developer having written everything up perfectly at release.

But expecting paper-level rigor for every new eval at launch would mean either delaying the evals until they're stale, or delaying launches indefinitely, and neither seems like a great outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says launch decisions happen before a new evaluation has time to mature into a polished research paper, while still arguing it should be included in launch reporting with caveats.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is just the timeline. When you write a paper on a new evaluation, you've typically spent months on it. You've iterated on the task design, you've run ablations, you've thought hard about what the results do and don't tell you, you've gotten feedback from colleagues who push back on your interpretation. That's what gives a paper its depth.

A model card or a frontier safety report doesn't get to work that way. The model is finished at a particular moment, and there's a fairly short window between that moment and launch. In that window you have to run all of your evaluations, not just one, and you have to write up the results for every single one of them. If you've got a dozen or more evaluations, and a few of them are new this cycle, there's just no way to give each of the new ones the equivalent of a research paper's worth of analysis. You'd have to delay the launch by months, and I don't think anyone is going to accept that for the sake of a more thorough write-up of one eval.

There's also a subtler issue, which is that a lot of what makes a paper-level treatment valuable is that you learn things about the evaluation itself by running it on many models over time. The first time you run a new eval on a frontier model, you often don't yet know how to interpret the result. Is this number high because the model is genuinely capable, or because there's some artifact in the task? You find that out by running it again, by looking at transcripts, by comparing across model generations. At launch you've typically run it exactly once on the model that matters, so your interpretation is necessarily provisional.

So the way I think about it is that the launch report should give you the result, a clear statement of what the evaluation was trying to measure, and an honest account of the limitations and the uncertainty in how we're reading it. The deeper treatment can come later, either in a paper or in an updated report, once we've actually had time to do that work. I'd much rather have that than have the launch report pretend to a level of confidence that we haven't earned yet.

r001.rationale: The response says launch reports can present an evaluation’s result and limitations before deeper analysis is done, but it does not clearly state that the evaluation is ready for decision making before it is ready for paper publication.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think they can’t in principle. It’s more that there’s a tension between the timing of a launch and the time it takes to do a really good scientific evaluation. You want to evaluate the actual model you’re releasing, and that model might only be available relatively shortly before launch. Meanwhile, for a new evaluation, you need to establish what it measures, check that the results are robust, understand the confounders, and work out what conclusions the results actually support. That’s a substantial research project.

So I’d distinguish reporting the results from validating the evaluation. You can report what you tested, how you tested it, and what happened in a model card. But giving a new evaluation the treatment you’d want in a paper requires a lot more work. Ideally, much of that validation happens beforehand, and you’re using an already well-understood evaluation at launch. Where that isn’t possible, I think you should be explicit about the uncertainty rather than treating the score as a definitive statement about safety.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes reporting results from fully validating a new evaluation, but it does not state that the evaluation can be ready for decision making substantially earlier than publication as a paper.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think they literally can’t. It’s more that there’s a tension between doing a really thorough scientific evaluation and having that evaluation inform a launch decision. If you’re developing a new evaluation for a frontier model, you may only get access to the final model fairly close to launch. And then you need to run the evaluation, understand the results, investigate surprising failures, and communicate what you found. Giving every new evaluation the treatment you’d give a standalone paper is a lot of additional work.

But I’d distinguish that from saying, “Therefore, we don’t need to provide evidence that the evaluation measures what we claim it measures.” You still need enough detail to make the result interpretable. If you’re using an evaluation to support a consequential safety claim, the standard of evidence should reflect that, whether or not the write-up looks like a paper.

r001.rationale: The response says a thorough paper-level evaluation takes additional work and may be difficult to complete near launch, but it does not clearly state that the evaluation can be ready for decision-making substantially earlier than it is ready for publication.
